newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvians approve Fujimori's tough speech in siege.
newsitem.headline: Peruvians approve Fujimori's tough speech in siege.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori's hard- line speech to Marxist rebels holding 340 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima received immediate support from the Peruvian public on Sunday.

"The position of rejecting all type of blackmail is correct," the country's leading analyst on terrorism, Carlos Tapia, told local radio. "Blackmail cannot be accepted and even less so the idea of freeing MRTA (Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement) rebels who would just return to their guerrilla activity."
Late on Saturday, Fujimori told the rebels in his first public statement since the crisis began that they must lay down their arms and free all their captives.
"I am in total agreement with what Fujimori said," independent congressman, Rafael Rey, said, reiterating the sentiment of calls to local radio by several legislators.

The president's speech also received praise for offering to study a non-violent "way out" should the rebels release their hostages, a glittering array of foreign diplomats, government officials and businessmen.
"Another possibility that did not exist has opened up and has left the option of another way out (of the crisis)," opposition congressman Alfonso Grados said.
"Despite the tough tone of the speech, there is the possibility of going forward in the negotiations," Tapia said.
Although the analyst said the talks over the siege, which started late on Tuesday, might drag on until 1997, he said the negotiations were "on the right path."

Fujimori's brief message, broadcast to the nation late on Saturday, was the government's first formal response to the guerrillas' threat that they would kill their hostages if up to 450 jailed comrades were not released.
The speech came only hours after Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela made a radio appeal from within the residence that the government establish a communication channel with the rebels.

"This is a strong position, just as it should be, because you cannot be weak," said nightwatchman Julio Policarpo. "However, it (the speech) also allows a dialogue. Without conversation they (the rebels) could begin a more drastic situation and sacrifice hostages."

While Fujimori has remained firm, rejecting the guerrillas' demands and refusing calls to reconnect electricity, water, and telephone services to the cramped residence, the guerrillas have given some ground.

First, they have released hostages - including a group of 38 diplomats, legislators and businessmen on Friday - and, second, they promised on Saturday to gradually free all captives who had no links with the government.
